nameStory: This humble plant earned the name 'pignut' because pigs would eagerly root through the soil to dig up its chestnut-like underground tubers. The connection to swine is so strong that it's also called 'Saint Anthony's nut' after Saint Anthony, the patron saint of pig farmers and swineherds.
description: Pignut is a perennial herb in the carrot family that looks much like its famous relatives - think Queen Anne's lace or wild carrot. It grows from an underground tuber that resembles a small chestnut and sends up delicate, feathery foliage topped with clusters of tiny white flowers arranged in umbrella-like patterns. The entire plant typically reaches 1-3 feet tall and has an overall delicate, lacy appearance.

idTips.label: Underground Tuber
idTips.description: The defining feature - a small, round, chestnut-like tuber buried 3-6 inches deep with dark brown skin and white, crisp flesh inside that's slightly sweet when raw

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers clustered in flat-topped umbrella shapes (umbels) typical of the carrot family, appearing delicate and lacy from a distance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Finely divided, feathery leaves that feel soft and delicate to the touch, resembling carrot tops but more finely cut

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a single stem or small clump from the underground tuber, with an overall delicate, wispy appearance that sways gently in breezes

habitat: Extremely rare in New England with only one documented observation - likely found in woodland edges, grasslands, or disturbed areas with well-drained soil. In its native European range, it prefers sandy or loamy soils in partial shade to full sun.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from the underground tuber, sending up fresh feathery foliage that's bright green and tender.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with clusters of tiny white flowers attracting small pollinators like flies and beetles.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves begin to yellow and die back, with energy returning to the underground tuber for winter storage.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant above ground - only the buried tuber remains alive, waiting for spring warmth to trigger new growth.

funFact: The underground tuber tastes remarkably like a cross between a chestnut and a radish - crisp and slightly peppery when raw, but sweet and nutty when cooked, making it a genuine 'wild potato' that was once cultivated as a crop in parts of Europe.
confusionNotes: With only one recorded sighting in New England, you're more likely to encounter similar-looking carrot family members like Queen Anne's lace or poison hemlock. The key difference is digging carefully to find pignut's distinctive chestnut-like tuber - but never eat any wild carrot family plant unless you're absolutely certain of the identification.
contextualKnowledge: Pignut shares many common names with other edible wild plants, including 'groundnut' and 'earthnut,' which can cause serious confusion. The name 'pignut' alone is used for several completely different plants across North America, so scientific names are crucial for accurate identification.
compareHints: Pignut is the only species in its genus (Conopodium) found in New England. Within the carrot family, it's most similar to other tuberous species, but differs from wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace) by having a round tuber rather than a taproot, and from poison hemlock by its much smaller, more delicate stature and edible underground parts.
